Sept. 1975 ERRATUM 1085
The photometric equations required to solve even simple problems
in photometry are not mentioned. The student who knows noth-
ing about photometry will not know much more after reading this
section; one who already knows enough to understand the section
does not need it. The same may be said of some other subjects
treated in this book, for instance the section on diffraction, where
the Huygens principle, Kirchhoff's law, the Rayleigh-Sommerfeld
equation, and Kottler's equations are disposed of in two pages.
Of the four pages devoted to the photographic emulsion, one is
dedicated to the bleaching of film, including a detailed recipe, but
the author forgot to say that this technique is used for holograms.
Holography is given an adequate treatment, except for some minor
deficiencies, such as discussions on recording parameters based on
the use of D vs log E curves instead of on the simpler use of T-E
curves, which are not mentioned.
The author has chosen to emphasize certain modern aspects of
optics, such as holography, optical correlators, side-looking radar,
and polarization in anisotropic media, at the expense of other
topics, such as integrated and fiber optics, and charge-coupled de-
vices, that you might expect to find in a book such as this. The
rationale for the choice of subjects included in the book is not
made clear.
The book contains many tables and charts, and discussions on
orders of magnitude. A lot of this information is difficult to find
gathered together, so you may find it useful to have the book on Charles Douglas Spencer

Dr. Anna Estelle Glancy, a member of the Optical Society for
47 years, died 19 May 1975 in Waltham, Massachusetts. For 33
years she was a lens designer in the research department of the
American Optical Corporation, where she designed special lenses,
and lenses for microscopes, cameras, and television systems.
Dr. Glancy received her B.A. from Wellesley College and her
Ph.D. in Astronomy from the University of California at Berkeley.
